title: Glen Canyon Dam serves storage, delivery, hydropower, drought buffer, and compact compliance purposes under CRSP authorization.
consolidated_finding: The source corpus establishes that Glen Canyon Dam and the Colorado River Storage Project were authorized in 1956 to provide long-term regulatory storage for Upper Colorado Basin compact delivery obligations, hydropower generation, and flood control. The extracted KU shows CRSP as the legal and operational foundation for all current drought response. In WY2026, drought buffer storage has become the dominant operational concern.
source_coverage_note: Supported by 1 KU from 1 source record: LP-DEMO-A-004.
notes: Minimal coverage of Operation Purpose in this 8-source corpus — expected for a focused drought-response source set.

title: WY2026 release rules layer three levels: Mid-Elevation Tier baseline, DROA 3,525 ft trigger, and Section 6.E emergency reduction to 6.0 maf.
consolidated_finding: Three overlapping rule layers govern Lake Powell WY2026 releases. First, the August 2025 24-Month Study set the Mid-Elevation Release Tier (January 1 elevation 3,525–3,575 ft) with a standard 7.48 maf release under Section 6.C.1. Second, the DROA was triggered when elevation was projected below 3,525 ft, establishing the 3,525 ft→3,490 ft operational buffer as a formal rule boundary. Third, DOI invoked Section 6.E emergency authority to cut the annual release to 6.0 maf — unprecedented under Mid-Elevation Tier conditions. The annual tier-locking mechanism (August Study sets the year's baseline, only Section 6.E can override mid-year) is the structural rule that governs how these three layers interact.
source_coverage_note: Supported by 4 KUs from 3 source records: LP-DEMO-A-001, LP-DEMO-A-002, LP-DEMO-A-004.
notes: The 7.48 maf vs 6.0 maf values are a status/sequencing difference, not a contradiction; see synthesis card SYN-LP-DEMO-005.

title: Dam infrastructure creates a three-layer hydraulic exit structure with critical elevations at 3,648 ft (spillways), 3,490 ft (penstocks), and 3,394 ft (river outlet works dead pool), with a practical redline at 3,500 ft.
consolidated_finding: Glen Canyon Dam has three water release pathways with discrete elevation thresholds: spillways at 3,648 ft (not relevant at current levels); eight 15-ft penstocks (incapacitated below 3,490 ft minimum power pool); and four 8-ft river outlet works at 3,370 ft dead pool (functionally limited at 3,394 ft, not designed for sustained use, and damaged during 2023 high-flow testing). Reclamation's operational redline is 3,500 ft — 10 ft above minimum power pool — because it cannot reliably operate the outlet works for extended periods. This redline strands 4.4 MAF below it (only 3.7 MAF accessible). The DROA 3,525 ft Target Elevation was specifically chosen to provide a 35-ft response buffer above the 3,490 ft hydropower floor. Additionally, WAPA's marketing of approximately 75% of CRSP Basin Fund revenue from Glen Canyon hydropower creates a binding constraint on release timing — minimizing Basin Fund impact is a formal DROA requirement.
source_coverage_note: Supported by 5 KUs from 3 source records: LP-DEMO-A-003, LP-DEMO-C-002, LP-DEMO-C-002, LP-DEMO-C-002, LP-DEMO-C-002.
notes: Infrastructure KUs are disproportionately sourced from TR-C (Circle of Blue); TR-A source verification of the 4.4 MAF and 3,500 ft engineering details is recommended before final dataset release.

title: 2026 DROA activation deployed three simultaneous measures: release reduction to 6.0 maf, 1.0 MAF Flaming Gorge draw, and monthly GCD adjustments — framed as 'reservoir triage.'
consolidated_finding: The 2026 drought response comprises three interlocked emergency measures executed simultaneously. First, Glen Canyon Dam releases were cut to 6.0 maf (the legal minimum, never before done). Second, the 2026 DROA Plan called for 660,000 AF–1.0 MAF of releases from Flaming Gorge with contingent contributions from Blue Mesa and Navajo; no recovery of released water is anticipated through the plan year. Third, the DROA operational sequencing requires monthly adjustments at GCD before upstream draws are made. These together represent 'reservoir triage' — a multi-lever emergency response that depletes upstream buffers and is characterized by experts as sustainable for only 'once or twice' before those buffers are exhausted. The May 2026 24-Month Study formally incorporated 1.0 MAF of DROA releases as model inputs, confirming real-time deployment.
source_coverage_note: Supported by 3 KUs from 3 source records: LP-DEMO-A-002, LP-DEMO-A-003, LP-DEMO-C-002.
notes: Expert 'once or twice' quote requires source verification against official DROA documents before treatment as authoritative.

title: DROA, 24-Month Study, Section 6.E, and WAPA coordination create a multi-layer governance architecture for drought response.
consolidated_finding: The coordination mechanisms governing WY2026 operations span multiple layers: (1) DROA provides the formal legal instrument for upstream CRSP Initial Unit releases, including operational sequencing (GCD monthly adjustments first) and accounting (credit/debit); (2) the annual tier-locking via the August 24-Month Study establishes the release framework for the entire year, requiring Section 6.E invocation for any mid-year override; (3) WAPA's power marketing obligations create a binding co-constraint on DROA release timing; (4) the Department of Interior retains independent emergency authority regardless of DROA. These layers are designed to activate in sequence rather than simultaneously, but WY2026 conditions have required all of them at once.
source_coverage_note: Supported by 3 KUs from 2 source records: LP-DEMO-A-002, LP-DEMO-A-003.
notes: Post-2026 Interim Guidelines replacement is not yet covered in this source corpus — a gap for future source acquisition.

title: WY2026 operational data: 3.27 maf inflow (34% of average), 3,510.85 ft year-end elevation, 4.77 maf storage (20% capacity) under most probable scenario.
consolidated_finding: The current operational state as captured in the source corpus: Lake Powell WY2026 inflow is forecast at 3.27 maf (34% of the 1991–2020 average), with a range of 2.95–4.27 maf (10th–90th percentile). Under the most probable scenario, the May 24-Month Study projects a year-end elevation of 3,510.85 ft with 4.77 maf in storage (20% of capacity). The total Colorado Basin system storage at the beginning of WY2026 was approximately 21.8 maf (37% of combined capacity). The period 2000–2025 represents the lowest 23-year average inflow since dam closure in 1963 (8.29 maf, 93% of average).
source_coverage_note: Supported by 2 KUs from 1 source record: LP-DEMO-A-001.
notes: Operational data is primarily sourced from LP-DEMO-A-001 (USBR operations page). LP-DEMO-A-002 (24-Month Study) provides additional tabular data not fully captured in the current KU set.

title: Research on forecast horizons confirms that large western US reservoirs routinely use long-range snowpack-based forecasts; models neglecting forecast horizon may underestimate drought risk.
consolidated_finding: A study of 300+ US dams (≥10 Mm³ storage) found approximately 80% use medium-to-long range inflow forecasts, with western high-elevation reservoirs using long-range horizons (>6 weeks) driven by snowpack. Simulation on four key western US reservoirs shows that forecast-informed models outperform models neglecting the forecast horizon, including during drought conditions. This has direct relevance to evaluating the 24-Month Study and CRSS models used for Lake Powell: if those models do not properly represent how forecast horizon shapes release decisions, their drought projections may be systematically optimistic — with implications for DROA activation timing.
source_coverage_note: Supported by 2 KUs from 1 source record: LP-DEMO-B-002. LP-DEMO-B-001 (modeling impacts report) was not acquired (77-char short content) — a gap in the research coverage.
notes: Research/Modeling coverage is thin due to LP-DEMO-B-001 acquisition failure. Recommend re-acquisition with paywall bypass or interlibrary access before final synthesis.

title: Inflow forecast range of 1.32 maf (2.95–4.27 maf) creates significant elevation uncertainty; structured probabilistic analysis is absent from the current source corpus.
consolidated_finding: The 10th–90th percentile inflow uncertainty range of 1.32 maf for WY2026 implies potentially large elevation outcomes at year-end, but the current KU set does not capture a probabilistic distribution of elevation outcomes from the 24-Month Study. The source corpus lacks: (1) month-by-month elevation projections under min/max probable scenarios; (2) the Lake Mead elevation coordination data relevant to cascading system effects; (3) any post-2026 rule development documents; (4) the LP-DEMO-B-001 modeling impacts document (acquisition failed). Additionally, the research in LP-DEMO-B-002 raises the question of whether the 24-Month Study and CRSS models properly account for forecast horizons in their release decision logic — a potential systematic bias in the primary operational model.
source_coverage_note: Supported by 2 KUs from 2 source records: LP-DEMO-A-001, LP-DEMO-B-002. Gaps are source-corpus evidence gaps, not workflow extraction limitations.
notes: This is a source-corpus evidence gap. Confirmed missing content includes LP-DEMO-B-001 (failed acquisition), Lake Mead coordination data, and Post-2026 rule development documents.
